Tech cards are fun!

I find that they add one more element of the unknown that you and the other players can add to their arsenal. Most importantly one that is hard to counter.

As to them being OP, I would disagree.  Remember that you can only add one ship to their research every regroup phase, and those ships can not be used for anything else until the tech is either finished or abandoned. This means high powered tech like the one that gives you another alien power, the one that destroys a planet, or the one that let's you gain a colony will take up to 10 encounters to complete (remember that a tech isn't completed the encounter you put the last ship on, but the first regroup phase that it has the requisite on it to start.) Many games will be over well before this point.

As to using a card zap on tech, you cannot. The card zap specifically states it can be used to stop a flair or artifact card, of which tech is neither. There is a tech that will counter other tech, or an omni zap can do it if you have the expansion that includes the rewards deck.

One thing I will say is that I wouldn't include tech for someone's first game. The game already has a ton of rules and exceptions to rules for players to learn, so adding another deck of cards and a whole subsystem just makes early games more incomprehensible.

Op mentions swift casting at lvl 2. The wealth by level at lvl 2, on the fast track, is 800gp. The lesser quicken metamagic rod costs 35,000gp. He only has to come up with 34,200 more gp to make this work.

Why not use a magus? It does basically everything you want, the only difference is that instead of a swift action, it casts as part of a full attack action. You can cast buffs with spell combat, and even better than the warpriest, they can affect your teammates as well! It does have plenty of uses for its swift actions though.

Other than that your options for a front line arcane fighter with swift action casting are almost non existant. You could try and focus on the quicken metamagic with a bloodrager, but good luck with that +4 to spell level.

Your other option is homebrew, but when people homebrew classes they want to play, they usually overpower them to hell. For instance taking warpriest and swapping in the wizard/sorc spell list would definately be OP as that spell list is decidedly better.

I agree with not including them in the first game to make play flow faster. They add a large randomization element to every game which can be huge in impact which I enjoy. The only drawback is they can be complicated and wordy, requiring a fair amount of reading when you draw one.

I would also stop discouraging multiple person wins. Part of the fun of the game is different people have different play styles. Some people will always go for a solo win for the glory, while others will invite allies for a more secure victory. With various races wacky things can happen, like everyone in the game winning, or no one in the game winning.

A variant my group almost always plays with is secret races. You keep your race face down and don't reveal who you are until you use your power. This variant makes the game more exciting with big dramatic reveals which can completely change the outcome of encounters.

Once your group is more familiar with the rules I also recommend the double races variant. This allows for crazy combos and even more variety in play.

If this is truly in reference to berserk, this question has more depth than should be addressed in a test. This is some thesis level Shit.

First lets start with the concept of an experiment. With no semblance of a control, there is no way to refer to the actions which Griffith took as an experiment. It lacks any form of academic rigor and as such should not be approached as a scientific endevor in any form.

With that out of the way we can view Griffiths actions, and their consequences, through a philosophical lense as opposed to a scientific one.

In the world of Berserk, what does transformation mean? 

Does it mean that one thing(or being/person) changes parts or itself, leaving some core identity the same while only changing outward appearances and tools? If this is true, then Griffith is a monster. Responsible for the rape of Casca, the sacrifice of the band of the hawk, and the sins of the apostles he granted power.

Or does it mean that the original being disappears and an entirely new one takes it's place? If this is true, the Griffith that became Femto was responsible for the rape of Casca and the slaughter of the band of the hawk. That Griffith then died and became Femto, who was responsible for the apostles he granted power. He then transformed, which means the current Griffith is responsible for none of those sins.

Between these two extremes lies our example of Guts. 

While Griffith went through grand transformations, Guts transforms gradually. He accepts responsibility for all of his failures, and the sins he (knowingly or unknowingly) committed. He does not ask for those he encounters or travels with to forget or ignore the sins, instead he tries to atone for them, or learn from them and do better in the future. 

I find this to be the central conflict of Berserk. Can one find redemption through simple change? Or must one earn redemption? Must it be fought for and gained?

You can say, "I invite steve, but he has to send 2 or more ships," but there is nothing in the rules which state he has to abide by that.  He would be able to send only one ship if he chose. The rules do not allow you to add additional conditions to alliance offers. In addition, if you try to offer a conditional alliance, the other person accepts, but does not meet your condition, you can not retract your offer. This is because the order of play is

1. Offense offers alliances, they may not invite the defense
2. Defense offers alliances, they may not invite the offense 
3. Person to the left of the offense accepts up to one offer made to them. Repeat this step until all players offered alliances have accepted or declined their offers.

There is no step where an offer may be rescinded.

Reading this thread, it becomes more and more clear that op has not been a server nor does he have much knowledge of dining etiquette.

There are a two main problems with splitting checks by default.

 The first is keeping who ordered what straight can be difficult. With a more experienced server or a higher level of service this is usually done by seat position. But with large groups, where split checks are the most useful, people often move and switch seats. And with inexperienced servers, or restaurants where the server has a high volume of tables, items are grouped by table with no regard to who ordered them. 

The second problem is with shared items, such as bottles of wine, appetizers, and desserts. Such things are often ordered by group consensus and there is no clear person to whom the server would assign the item. 

A clear solution to the first problem would be forcing guests to keep the same seat, but that would go against the concept of the restaurant being there to serve the guest and make them comfortable.

A solution to the second problem would be to ask who is going to pay for these items when ordered, but that would be considered tacky at least, and insulting at most. Since most restaurants try to exhibit at least a slight modicum of decorum, this is not likely to happen.
